prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures an elevated playground scene where a child starts very close on the left (brightest white, ~0.2–0.4 m from the camera wearer) in Frames 1–2, looking right in profile toward a bright tan slide entrance (~0.5–0.8 m ahead on the right) that sits within the camera wearer's arm's reach and in front of a mid-grey left wall (~1.0–1.5 m) and overhead canopy (~1.5–2.0 m above). Across Frames 3–5, the child moves rightward into the center foreground (~0.4–0.7 m away) while reaching up to grasp the horizontal bar at the top of the slide opening within arm's reach, before crouching down and retreating into the recessed tunnel in Frame 5 (~0.8–1.2 m away, darker grey) with their back to the camera wearer and lower body occluded inside the chute. Compared to the RGB strip, the depth map makes it much easier to see the smooth concave recession of the shadowed slide interior, the spatial separation between the child's backlit profile and the background in Frames 1–2, and the depth of the secondary tunnel opening on the left in Frame 3. However, the map is unreliable for the distant yard, trees, and houses visible through the slide opening and above the walls—which are flattened to uniform pitch black (>5 m)—and in Frame 3 where the child's raised right arm merges in brightness with the adjacent slide housing.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates the child (`person` mask in pink) moving from the left foreground (~0.2–0.4 m from the camera wearer, cropped at the bottom and left edges) in Frames 1–2 to the center (~0.4–0.7 m) in Frames 3–4 and into the right-side slide opening (~0.8–1.2 m) in Frame 5, while always facing right or away from the camera wearer. In Frames 2, 4, and 5, it also segments parts of the moulded plastic playground structure within the camera wearer's arm's reach (~0.5–0.8 m) directly in front of and around the child, showing the child overlapping the front of the structure in Frames 3–4 and partially occluded inside the opening in Frame 5. The masks help distinguish the exact contour of the child's shadowed face in Frames 1–2 and separate the child's crouching back and right arm from the dark tunnel interior in Frame 5, which are hard to discern in the RGB shadows. However, the map is highly unreliable for scene objects and boundaries: it mislabels the slide entrance as a `parking meter` in Frame 2 and as `car` instances in Frames 4–5, omits the slide entirely in Frames 1 and 3 as well as the blue posts and overhead roof throughout, and merges the space between the child's torso and right arm into the `person` mask in Frame 3.
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks the child's orientation and movement only intermittently across the black canvas, showing a small cluster of yellow head keypoints on the left (~0.3–0.4 m away, facing right and away from the camera wearer) in Frame 2, an upper-body and arm skeleton in the center (~0.5–0.7 m away) in Frame 4, and a crouched upper-body skeleton inside the right-side tunnel (~0.8–1.2 m away) in Frame 5. Between Frames 4 and 5, the skeleton shifts downward and rightward away from the camera wearer, capturing the child transitioning from an upright torso with the right arm bent upward—placing magenta hand keypoints on the overhead grab bar within both the child's and camera wearer's arm's reach—to a forward-leaning posture with the right arm angled down into the slide opening. In Frame 4, the magenta hand skeletons clearly resolve the overlapping positions of both hands gripping the shadowed underside of the bar, and the yellow torso line indicates the hip position even though the lower body is cropped out of view. However, the pose map is unreliable in Frames 1 and 3 where it completely fails to detect the close-up head and the reaching child in the center, and in Frames 4–5 where the occluded lower limbs and left arm skeleton are missing alongside the entire playground structure.
